---
title: "Tree Search"
description: "A search strategy that explores possible future states by expanding a tree of choices."
term: "Tree Search"
letter: "T"
category: "Algorithms"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Tree search explores choices by representing them as branches. Each path
corresponds to a sequence of decisions, and the algorithm expands promising
branches to find a goal or a high-value outcome.

## Technical explanation

A search tree has nodes representing states and edges representing actions.
Algorithms such as breadth-first search, depth-first search, and
Monte Carlo tree search differ in how they expand nodes, manage memory, and
prioritize exploration. Search quality depends on branching factor,
depth, costs, and any heuristic or rollout policy.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Tree search is used in planning, games, program synthesis, and reasoning
systems. It offers explicit exploration of alternatives but can grow
exponentially, so practical systems use pruning, heuristics, or compute
budgets.

## How it works

The algorithm starts from an initial state, selects a node to expand,
generates successor states, and tracks paths or values. It stops when it
finds a goal, reaches a depth or resource limit, or determines a best
available action.

## Practical example

A game-playing program can search future move sequences and evaluate
resulting positions. It may prioritize branches using a heuristic or
sampled outcomes, then choose a move within a fixed compute budget.

## Common misconceptions

- Tree search does not guarantee an optimal result if depth, branching,
  evaluation, or time is limited.
- A state-space tree can contain repeated states; implementations may use
  caching or graph-search techniques to avoid redundant work.
